questions.q: In the Azure SQL Database resource hierarchy, what does the logical server own versus what the database owns?
options: The server owns the admin login, firewall rules, and DNS name; the database owns its own compute/storage tier and backup retention settings
The server owns backup retention; the database owns the admin login and firewall rules
They own identical settings — there's no real split between them
The server owns table schemas; the database owns the subscription and resource group
questions.explain: The logical server is a management boundary (admin login, firewall, DNS name); the database itself owns its tier and backup settings, which is why some settings live at one level and some at the other.

questions.q: Why does the server name (sql-overlook-capstone) need to be globally unique across all of Azure?
options: Because it becomes part of the public DNS name (<server-name>.database.windows.net)
Because Azure only allows one SQL server per subscription
Because duplicate names cause billing conflicts
Because the name is used as the database's primary key
questions.explain: The server name is embedded in a globally resolvable DNS name, so it must be unique worldwide — which is why real deployments use a specific naming convention instead of a generic word.

questions.q: Why is General Purpose chosen as the service tier for Overlook's database in this lesson?
options: It's the standard vCore tier sized appropriately for a real but modest workload, without over- or under-provisioning
It's the only tier that supports automated backups
It's required for any database storing patient data
It's the cheapest tier available regardless of workload
questions.explain: General Purpose is the standard production tier for workloads that don't need Premium's higher I/O or Hyperscale's massive-scale storage — an honest fit for a single provider network's scheduling and billing database.

questions.q: Why does the lesson create a firewall rule allowing only one specific IP address, rather than enabling 'Allow Azure services'?
options: It's the narrower, more defensible default — opening exactly the one connection needed instead of a broad allowance
Azure SQL Database doesn't support the 'Allow Azure services' option
A single-IP rule is required before the database can be created at all
Firewall rules only apply to SQL Server on a VM, not Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: Scoping the firewall rule to exactly your own IP is the narrower, more defensible choice for this project rather than opening broader access than is actually needed.

questions.q: What real backup consequence has already been decided by choosing Azure SQL Database (PaaS) instead of SQL Server on an Azure VM?
options: Microsoft takes automated full/differential/log backups on its own schedule — you don't run a raw BACKUP DATABASE statement against it
Backups become entirely optional and can be skipped
Only full backups are possible; differential and log backups aren't available
Backup retention must be configured manually to even 1 day, the shortest retention
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database is a PaaS tier where Microsoft owns the backup mechanism and schedule — a real, accurate platform behavior that shapes what the next several lessons in this capstone actually look like.
